newsitem.title: GERMANY: Belarus-Russia union no threat - German experts.
newsitem.headline: Belarus-Russia union no threat - German experts.

text.p: A union treaty signed on Wednesday by Russia and Belarus is more a tactical move by President Boris Yeltsin than a sign of Russian expansionism, and does not represent a direct threat to the West, German experts say.

Germany's geographical position in the centre of Europe makes it particularly sensitive to the balance of power to the east, leading it to argue for a Russian role in European security but also for the eastward enlargement of NATO.

Extending Russia's influence westward lets Yeltsin argue at home that he is reacting to NATO expansion, even if the union project does not eventually lead to an alliance of much substance, the experts said on Wednesday.
"If anything, this move may pacify the communists and nationalists and give Yeltsin the space to press on with economic reforms," said Hermann Clement of the East European Institute in Munich.

"I don't see a threat in it for Germany and Western Europe, although it may make Poland a little nervous. It may also persuade some countries such as Ukraine or the Baltic states to try to push harder to get into NATO."

Several analysts note that an economic link-up with Belarus and its weak, still largely state-owned economy is likely to be a burden to Russia, while in military terms Moscow has little to gain apart from making a symbolic statement.
Heinz Timmermann of the Federal Institute for Eastern Studies in Cologne noted that Russia already has control of a planned gas pipeline intended to run west across Belarus.
It also has several strategic installations -- missile defence systems and electronic information gathering -- located on Belarussian territory and manned by Russian soldiers.

"To most Russians, union with Belarus will be an effective response to NATO enlargement. Russia can use Belarus as a bargaining chip ahead of the Madrid summit where NATO plans to invite applications from new members," Alexander Rahr of the German Foreign Policy Society told German radio.
"Russian politicians can say that if the West were to decide to put nuclear weapons in Poland or Hungary, then Russia will also be able to put them on the Polish border, in Belarus."

But Rahr said that in practice, little would change for the West, as Belarus had always belonged to Moscow's sphere of influence, even after it gained independence with the collapse of the Soviet Union.
"The union treaty doesn't represent a new threat for the West," he said.

"Belarus was never 100 percent independent. Russia's military command has always had a big influence on the Belarus army, and Belarus is utterly dependent on the Russian economy and military-industrial complex. So from that point of view, not very much has changed."

Germany has already frozen some restructuring aid to Belarus in protest at what it saw as Lukashenko's undemocratic methods of shoring up his power, and will be keen that he should not achieve his stated objective of gaining influence in Moscow.
"Yeltsin may be getting more than he's bargained for in forging links with someone who has been an economic failure, is politically dictatorial and is extremely unpredictable," Timmermann said.
